chapter: Radio, theaters and early dance forms
title: Directing the Liberty Theatre orchestra and playing for silent pictures
summary: DeDroit describes his vocalist Miss Durio, then the theater orchestras, his eight men at the Liberty, song slides and picture music libraries.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Can I see that picture for a second? So that's more of a character? That's uh, Miss Durio,
Durio, she's an operatic singer. She was my vocalist on big jobs. That's more, that, uh, the New Leviathan
arrangement is more of something that's characteristic of the theaters, you'd say, than the dance jobs? No, no, no.
It's characteristic of a stock arrangement with fiddles, you know what I mean? It sounds, it has to, it has to. Where would,
where would one have found that sort of thing mostly back in the, say, the twenties? Where would you find it?

Mostly, yeah. Where would you? Well, you'd find any of the shows that had orchestras big enough to play something, but they also played for the pictures, you know what I mean? Yeah. We used to have to feature the pictures. Yeah. I only had eight men at the Liberty when I was directing the orchestra at the Liberty, and I used to play pop tunes all the time for the Overtures, but I used to, sometimes I'd throw slides and invite the audience to sing. And I had a couple of friends who liked to sing, and I'd take the lunch hour and I'd put the song on, because I wanted to holler and light and yell. I had a guy, a broker, used to leave his office and come over and sing. Where was this at? At the Liberty. It's a parking lot now.
Oh, more progress. Yeah, more progress.
We'd chase pictures every weekend. I had a feature picture every weekend. But they furnished us, we had a beautiful library called Galaxy of Picture Music. And you could get music to fit most any
scene. So the theater's one place you'd hear. Where else did you?
